Slumberings
SLUM-ber-ings
n. pl. (light sleeps; drowsings upon the bed)
From slumber, Middle English slumeren, from Old English sluma, light sleep. The Hebrew tenumah means slumber or drowsiness, distinguished from deep sleep.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Elihu answers Job's complaint that God does not speak by listing the ways He does: “In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed” (Job 33:15). Slumberings are light sleeps, the drowsing state at the edge of unconsciousness, and the whole verse insists that God addresses men where they are least in control of themselves. Elihu's premise is stated first: “For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not” (Job 33:14). The fault is not in God's silence but in man's dullness. And the stated purpose of the night-speaking is instruction and rescue: “Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction” (Job 33:16), that He may withdraw man from his purpose and hide pride from him. The dictionary notes carefully what this does and does not establish. In the patriarchal age, before the canon was complete, God did speak by dreams and visions, and Scripture records it without apology. With the canon closed, the Spirit speaks in and by the written Word, and no slumbering now brings revelation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): SLUMBER, to sleep lightly; to doze; SLUMBERING, light sleep; a dozing.

SLUMBER, v.i. To sleep lightly; to doze; to be in the state between sleeping and waking.

SLUMBER, n. Light sleep; sleep not deep or sound.

SLUMBERING, ppr. Dozing; sleeping lightly.

Hebrew tenumah, slumber or drowsiness, as distinct from deep sleep.

Job 33:15 speaks of God addressing men in slumberings upon the bed.

Key Scripture

Job 33:15 — "In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed;"

Job 33:14 — "For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not."

Job 33:16 — "Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction,"

Modern Corruption

Dreams are treated as a live channel of fresh revelation for the church today, which sets private impressions beside the completed Scriptures.

expand to see more

Charismatic and prophetic movements cite Job 33:15 and Joel 2 to establish dreams and night visions as a continuing means by which God delivers new messages, and the practical result is a stream of personal revelations that nobody can test and that routinely contradict one another. The dictionary holds the sufficiency of Scripture: the canon is closed, and what God has to say to His church He has said in the Book.

The opposite error is to deny that God ever spoke so, or to be embarrassed by the patriarchal narratives. Scripture reports them as fact. Joseph, Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Joseph the husband of Mary and Paul at Troas all received genuine communications in the night, and Hebrews marks the change of administration precisely: God who spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. Elihu's point survives the change of means intact: God speaks, and man's problem is that he perceiveth it not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From slumber, Old English sluma, light sleep; Hebrew tenumah; Job 33:15 names slumberings upon the bed.

expand to see more

Old English sluma, light sleep, gives slumber and slumbering.

Hebrew tenumah, slumber or drowsiness, distinct from deep sleep.

Job 33:15 is the only occurrence of slumberings in the Authorized Version.

Elihu's premise is that God speaks and man perceiveth it not.

The stated purpose is to seal instruction and to hide pride from man.
